item.title: Google's AI-generated search summaries reduce clicks to external websites by about 40%, study finds [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A randomized experiment found that Google's AI-generated Overviews appearing in search results cut clicks to outside websites by nearly 40% among US desktop users. These AI summaries now appear on over 60% of US keywords tracked, up from under 6% two years ago, significantly impacting organic traffic to websites. The study observed that searches with AI Overviews had a higher rate of no outbound clicks, while ad clicks remained stable, indicating Google's revenue was unaffected. The research, based on a controlled trial and observational data, focused on informational searches and covered desktop users in the US during early 2026. It also noted that the rise of AI Overviews has coincided with declines in traditional featured snippets and forum results. The findings suggest that while SEO remains important, the emergence of generative engine optimization (GEO) is still developing as a strategy to adapt to AI-driven search changes.

item.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models with enhanced capabilities
item.description: OpenAI has introduced GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, the latest versions of its language models designed to improve performance and versatility. These models aim to advance natural language understanding and generation across various applications. The release marks a continued effort by OpenAI to refine AI capabilities and expand their practical use cases.

item.title: Microsoft introduces MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash cybersecurity products with enhanced security and lower cost
item.description: Microsoft announced the launch of MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash, new cybersecurity solutions designed to provide leading security features while reducing costs. The announcement was made on November 17, 2026, highlighting the company's focus on advancing security technology with cost efficiency. These products aim to address evolving cybersecurity challenges by combining robust protection capabilities with affordability, targeting organizations seeking effective security solutions without excessive expense.

item.title: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents increased code output by 30% but extended code review time by 49%, shifting the development bottleneck [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton analyzed data from 718 firms using AI coding agents and found that while engineers produced about 30% more code, the time to complete code reviews increased by 49%, resulting in no measurable rise in finished work. Their study, based on data from Jellyfish and LinkedIn employment records, covers activity from January 2021 to March 2026 and uses a staggered difference-in-differences approach to compare early and late adopters of AI tools. The researchers note that procurement delays and firm size were controlled for in their analysis, and the findings suggest that AI accelerates drafting but shifts the bottleneck to human review stages. The study highlights implications for legal and compliance professionals using AI tools, emphasizing the need to measure approved work product and reviewer time alongside drafting output. The paper is a working paper without completed peer review and focuses on software development rather than legal work.

item.title: Runta and Baseten release FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 leaderboard evaluating 22 harnesses across 5 models and 62 tasks to identify best harness-model pairs by cost and pass rate [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Runta partnered with Baseten to create FrontierHarness Eval v1.1, a large-scale benchmark evaluating 22 harness configurations across five AI models and 62 tasks, totaling over 27,000 agent runs and 83 billion tokens. The study aimed to determine whether switching harnesses when changing models improves performance and cost efficiency, finding that the best harness varies significantly by model. The evaluation measured average cost per task and pass rates, revealing that harnesses optimal for one model may perform poorly with another. For example, Codex CLI was most cost-effective with GLM-5.3 but ranked much lower with other models. The benchmark identified top harnesses for each model based on cost per pass, highlighting trade-offs between cost and accuracy. The results suggest users should consider changing harnesses alongside models to maximize value and performance.

item.title: Researchers identify that continuing reasoning after a correct answer can reduce accuracy in AI models, analyzing commitment-verdict gaps and stopping rules on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers demonstrate that AI reasoning models can lose correct answers by overthinking, as the final verdict alone cannot predict whether continuing reasoning improves or harms accuracy. They introduce a framework comparing the model's current commitment to its final verdict, revealing that the difference predicts potential accuracy changes and informs optimal stopping decisions. Experiments on six reasoning models across MATH-500 and OlympiadBench datasets show that continuing reasoning after a correct answer often decreases accuracy, with an oracle stopping rule providing limited gains. This work clarifies what metrics to measure before designing stopping rules to prevent harmful overthinking in AI reasoning chains.

item.title: SkillBuffBench benchmark evaluates agent Skills across harnesses, models, skill access modes, and memory on research tasks in materials science and biology [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: SkillBuffBench is a new benchmark and evaluation protocol designed to measure the contribution of agent Skills-file-based procedural knowledge packages-across different agent harnesses, models, skill access modes, and memory settings. It tests state-of-the-art proprietary and open-weight models from providers like Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and Chinese companies, running each model under four harnesses on tasks contributed by domain experts in materials science and biology. The benchmark treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, curated Skill, automatic invocation) and evaluates performance with deterministic verification, reporting uncertainty, cost, agent rounds, and wall-clock time alongside scores. The benchmark's evaluation is ongoing, with results to be added as runs complete and the task suite and analysis updated continuously. This version of the paper details the benchmark's design, evaluation protocol, and current tasks and Skills, aiming to provide a comprehensive and realistic assessment of how agent Skills contribute in deployment scenarios where agents select from installed libraries and retain memory from prior work.

item.title: Researchers introduce token commitment as a control surface for steering masked diffusion models, proposing counterfactual target-aware commitment and adaptive budgets to improve target-quality trade-offs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose treating token commitment-the decision of which provisional tokens become permanent and how many to commit at each step-as a control surface for steering masked diffusion models. They introduce counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks unresolved positions based on model confidence and token contribution, and calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence. These methods were tested across language and vision-language tasks in the LLaDA family and on the Dream-7B model, showing consistent improvements in target-quality trade-offs and applicability to automatic proxies for task success such as NLI entailment and CLIPScore. The study demonstrates that these commitment mechanisms require only a scalar score evaluated on provisional completions, allowing them to function without predefined steering directions. Adaptive schedules also matched or outperformed scorer-free stochastic schedules in terms of denoising cost. The results characterize token commitment as an interpretable and effective control mechanism for masked diffusion generation under the tested conditions.

item.title: Researchers analyze 14 language models to distinguish moral evaluation circuits from cue word responses using 227 phrase pairs across moral and normative judgments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied 14 open-weight language models, including Llama, Gemma, and Qwen, to identify attention heads and sparse autoencoder features that influence moral judgments in prompts. They tested 227 minimal phrase pairs differing in moral standards, other norms, or descriptive qualities, with and without the word "morally," finding that the same evaluation circuits handle moral and other normative judgments equally across models. The study showed these evaluation heads are essential even when no explicit judgment is requested, significantly affecting model responses on the ETHICS benchmark scenarios. Sparse autoencoder features primarily responded to the presence of the word "morally" rather than the phrase content. The models encode normative categories in their hidden states, and removing these directions weakens moral verdicts more than other judgments in most tested models. The researchers released their data, code, and trained models for further analysis.

item.title: Researchers introduce EJBench, a software-agnostic benchmark testing engineering judgement on conjugate heat transfer design for battery cold plates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: EJBench evaluates whether models can predict design behavior under new conditions using limited prior results, without running simulations. The benchmark includes tasks such as matching unlabelled test results to operating points, selecting stored runs for design approval, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature, all based on converged simulation data rather than language model judgement. The best-performing model, GPT-6 Astra, achieved a score of 0.71, while post-training Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning improved its score from 0.071 to 0.106 on a held-out test set. The researchers have released the dataset splits, evaluation tools, and leaderboard to support further development and comparison.

item.title: Researchers profile and optimize the sampling pipeline in 26B-parameter MoE diffusion language models, achieving up to 2.7x decoding speedup on NVIDIA GB10 without accuracy loss [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers analyzed the decoding process of a 26-billion-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model on a bandwidth-limited NVIDIA GB10 edge accelerator and found that after weight quantization, the logits sampling pipeline, rather than expert GEMMs, dominated decode time. Unlike autoregressive models, diffusion decoding processes multiple times more logits per output token due to iterative denoising steps. The team developed two lossless optimizations-a bit-exact tier and an accuracy-parity tier using fused entropy kernels and Gumbel-max sampling-that removed redundant computations and improved decoding speed by 2.4 to 2.7 times without affecting benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH datasets.

item.title: Researchers introduce Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model to capture document and section hierarchies in embedding space, improving topic coherence and clustering across structured text collections [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present the Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model (hETM), a structured topic model that links topic distributions of documents and their sections through a hierarchical prior in embedding space. This approach addresses the limitation of traditional embedded topic models that represent each document with a single topic distribution, ignoring internal hierarchical structure common in legal documents, reports, and forums. The team developed an amortized variational inference method for hETM and tested it on various structured datasets. Experimental results show that hETM achieves the lowest or near-lowest held-out perplexity compared to flat and hierarchical baselines, with comparable or better topic quality. It also outperforms other models in downstream clustering tasks on most collections, demonstrating its effectiveness in modeling hierarchical document structures.

item.title: Researchers propose RLDE, a reinforcement learning framework for interpretable iterative document editing that improves readability and preserves semantics with low computational cost [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce RLDE, an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that models document revision as a Markov decision process using limited editing actions and optimizes for readability, perplexity, and grammar without relying on paired revision targets. RLDE employs Pointer Networks for token-level span selection and a frozen BART-base model for context-aware suggestions, with a novel semantic preservation penalty to maintain meaning during edits. Evaluations on the BEA-2019 dataset show significant improvements in readability and perplexity while preserving 93% of semantic content, outperforming Chain-of-Thought prompt-engineered models like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2 at a lower inference cost. Human evaluations rated RLDE's edits highly for meaning preservation and quality.

item.title: Researchers show large language models can design efficient weight-space programs without transformers, achieving comparable accuracy with far fewer parameters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers explored weight-space programming where large language models (LLMs) generate neural network weights directly without gradient-based training, questioning the necessity of transformer architectures. They tasked three advanced LLMs with either generating weights for fixed architectures or designing architectures themselves, mainly on multiple-choice question tasks. When allowed to design freely, the LLMs created sparse table-based models that reached up to 54.4% test accuracy, outperforming transformer models written by the same LLM while using about 1,800 times fewer parameters. The study found that without gradients, LLMs preferred associative-memory-based models that allow explicit interpretation and correction of weights, leading to models up to 17 times faster on GPUs than similarly sized transformers. While pretrained LLMs remain more accurate overall, the findings suggest alternative architectures may be more suitable for weight-space programming where weights are written directly rather than trained with gradients.

item.title: NVIDIA post-trains Nemotron 3.5 Super with reinforcement learning on expert-built tasks, improving performance across 12 benchmarks including software engineering and document reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: NVIDIA applied reinforcement learning to post-train its Nemotron 3.5 Super model using five expert-built task datasets covering software engineering, complex constraints, tool use, chart understanding, and document reasoning. Each training run used a fresh LoRA adapter without supervised stages, and the adapters were evaluated against the base model on the same tasks and settings, showing significant performance gains on twelve benchmarks. The improvements ranged from 4.5 to 13.8 points across various benchmarks such as IFBench, GDP_pdf, SWE-bench Pro V2, Terminal-Bench 2.1, MultiChallenge, AutomationBench, and Chartography. The adapters demonstrated enhanced capabilities like better data and rule identification, test file generation, context retention, precise chart measurement, and spreadsheet reading compared to the base model.

item.title: OfficePrism benchmarks AI agents on 420 single-domain enterprise tasks across seven business functions with pass rates from 22.6% to 76.4% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OfficePrism evaluates AI agent performance on 420 single-domain tasks spanning seven enterprise business functions, using a shared synthetic organization and function-specific domains. The benchmark includes tasks structured at three levels (L1-L3) and uses a pipeline that generates Chinese-language tickets, executable reference witnesses, and expected responses, followed by automated filtering and human curation. Across 124 model and package configurations, pass rates vary from 22.6% to 76.4%, with the highest success at the simplest task level (L1) and better performance at level 2 compared to level 3 in most cases. The study compares full-schema and search-and-dispatch evaluation packages, finding search outperforms full-schema in 30 of 50 comparable configurations.

item.title: Researchers introduce ICA Lens to identify interpretable non-Gaussian directions in language model activations, demonstrating efficiency and competitive performance across GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B, and Qwen 3.5 9B Base [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed ICA Lens, a workflow that directly discovers non-Gaussian directions in large language model residual-stream activations without training sparse dictionaries. Testing on GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B, and Qwen 3.5 9B Base, they found these directions capture coherent lexical, syntactic, and semantic patterns, correlating with human and automated interpretability measures. ICA Lens achieves comparable results to sparse autoencoders while using significantly less memory and computation time, highlighting non-Gaussianity as a direct unsupervised signal for interpretable feature discovery in language models.

item.title: Researchers introduce Localized LoRA-MoE combining spatial blocking with context-conditioned expert routing to improve parameter-efficient fine-tuning across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present Localized LoRA-MoE, a framework that integrates localized spatial blocking with adaptive, context-conditioned routing to address gradient interference in parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA. They propose two variants-Block-Wise LoRA-MoE with centralized routing and Cell-Wise LoRA-MoE with decentralized routing-and evaluate them on structured transformation benchmarks, showing improved performance over static baselines under similar adapter budgets. The study demonstrates that both variants perform comparably when context shifts uniformly, while cell-wise routing excels in spatially heterogeneous contexts. Fine-tuning a language model on six interleaved GLUE tasks, task-conditioned routing outperforms LoRA and static adapters at fixed budgets, matching per-task adapters with six times the budget. At decoder scale on Qwen2.5-1.5B, both variants surpass static baselines across eight commonsense benchmarks, with cell-wise routing achieving a 3.9-point improvement over LoRA at matched active capacity.

item.title: Researchers identify simulator collapse in multi-agent reinforcement learning with single LLM simulators and propose Verbalized Sampling and Co-Training to improve generalization and policy diversity [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers found that multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) agents trained against a single large language model (LLM) simulator often fail to generalize due to simulator collapse, where the simulator exhibits mode collapse and the agent learns narrow strategies that do not transfer well to other simulators or real users. They formalized this issue and proposed two solutions: Verbalized Sampling, which samples simulator replies from a response distribution at inference time, and Co-Training, which co-evolves the simulator and policy during training to prevent exploitation of mode behavior. The team validated these methods on three benchmarks-Persuasion for Good, tau^2-bench, and CooperBench-showing that Verbalized Sampling improved held-out success rates by up to 9%, while Co-Training increased gains to 14%, with similar improvements observed in a human study. Both approaches also maintained policy diversity that typically collapses under single-simulator training. They released SCOPE, an open-source framework for Population Co-Training in multi-agent RL, highlighting the importance of diverse simulators for developing RL agents that effectively serve real users.

item.title: Researchers introduce SarcasTraps, a Turkish test set to evaluate sarcasm's impact on hate speech detection, revealing challenges for fine-tuned models and zero-shot LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed SarcasTraps, a dataset of 479 Turkish entries annotated for hate speech and sarcasm, to study how sarcasm affects hate speech detection. They trained classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on existing datasets and tested them alongside GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in zero-shot settings. The results show sarcasm significantly reduces recall in fine-tuned models and lowers precision in zero-shot large language models, indicating both struggle with sarcastic hate speech. SarcasTraps will be available for academic research upon request due to its sensitive content.

item.title: Chain-of-Thought Controllability Can Reduce Chain-of-Thought Monitorability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. Averaged across evaluations and CoT lengths, weighted by side-task-success counts, the CoT monitorability metric g-mean$^2$ falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 for the model organism without a hiding instruction, and to 0.22 when explicitly instructed to hide. In intervention evaluations, explicit hiding often drives monitorability near zero. The effect extends to a Kimi-K2.6 model organism in agentic environments, though hidden objectives requiring extended reasoning or longer trajectories remain more monitorable than simple single-step side tasks. We further discover that targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability, sometimes surpassing the base model. These model organisms provide a testbed for studying monitorability failures and potential mitigations. Our code can be found on https://github.com/yongzx/cot-control-model-organism.

item.title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.

item.title: On Formal Counterfactual Explanations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Counterfactual explanations are often seen as counterfactual conditionals under closest-world semantics, requiring one to reason over all minimally distant counterexamples. In contrast, formal XAI typically relies on feature-based abductive explanations (AXps) and contrastive explanations (CXps), which admit efficient computation and a minimal hitting-set duality. This paper bridges these perspectives by (i) characterizing closest-world counterfactual explanations explicitly as a disjunctive normal form over all minimally distant counterexample instances, and (ii) introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps), a subclass of counterfactual antecedents restricted to conjunctions of feature literals that guarantee prediction change. The paper establishes structural results connecting CXps, AXps and CFXps: every CXp induces an AXp for its witness instance, and every CXp together with a witness AXp induces a CFXp whose support is precisely determined by that AXp. These theoretical results yield a modular approach for computing CFXps using existing AXp/CXp machinery. Experiments on a representative set of benchmarks using tree ensembles and neural networks show that CFXp extraction is practically efficient. Compared with popular point-based counterfactual explainers, CFXps generally require no more feature changes and can guarantee the counterfactual prediction beyond a single instance.

item.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22033v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

item.title: MedGuardBench: A Patient-Oriented Benchmark for Personalized Guardrail Development [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22069v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety is personal: the same action can be safe for one person but unsafe for another. Yet current guardrails judge content without considering who is affected. Using medication safety, we introduce \textit{patient-conditioned medication guarding}, which predicts a safety verdict and 17 risk categories from a patient profile and prescription. We release \textbf{MedGuardBench}, a drug-disjoint benchmark of 5{,}001 scenarios across 87 medications. We find that standard guardrails rely on surface cues, such as wording and profile presence, rather than patient facts. To address this, we develop \textit{personalized reasoning guardrails} with three components. \textbf{Personalized Reasoning Distillation} links risks to relevant patient fields. \textbf{Context Unrolling (CU)} makes models check each field themselves, reducing false alarms on most backbones; controls show that providing the check does not yield the same benefit. A \textbf{rule-based reward (guided GRPO)} improves unsafe recall and complex-risk detection, including allergies and adverse reactions, on some backbones, but increases false alarms on others. Our models outperform base models and matched no-profile controls in accuracy, while reducing false alarms relative to no-profile controls. Profile removal and swapping confirm that gains come from patient information, not fine-tuning alone.

item.title: LoCaR: Localized Canvas Retrieval With Frozen Vision-Language Model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whole image embeddings can under represent small objects and local attributes that distinguish relevant images for localized queries. We present LoCaR, a training free framework for localized text to image retrieval with frozen vision language models. LoCaR constructs and utilizes independent proposals (SAM2) focusing on the object so as to get a more localized representation that independently encodes each region using the frozen visual encoder. We further study paired-support adaptation as an optional residual that uses matched text region exemplars without updating the underlying encoders. We also introduce LOCFG, a Visual Genome derived benchmark designed to evaluate localized retrieval for smaller and more challenging referents. Across several vision language backbones, our results show that improving the region representation itself is the main source of gain.

item.title: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat) [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. We test 29 open-weight models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten established benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, covering SWE-bench Verified coding agents, long chain-of-thought reasoning, long-form writing, long structured output and long-context reading. Samplers that keep their pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises don't lose accuracy. Samplers that let in low-probability tokens fall apart. At temperature 2, coding agents running top-p, top-k or Top-H resolve 0 of 100 GitHub issues, while the same agents running top-nsigma resolve 46 to 62 and win every issue the two samplers disagree on, on three Qwen3.5 models. Over all benchmarks top-nsigma keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score where top-p keeps 26%. Counting how many tokens each sampler lets through explains why. In one Llama-3.1-8B story, going from temperature 1 to 2 grows top-p's pool from 4 tokens to 51,845 while top-nsigma stays at 3. Across 133 combinations of sampler setting and temperature, the typical pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation of -0.77), and when we pick the pool at temperature 1 and only apply temperature afterwards, Top-H, min-p and p-less stop collapsing. At the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same, We release all code and data to the public.

item.title: Fine-Grained Japanese Clinical Named Entity Recognition: A Controlled Comparison of BERT and Open-Weight Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background: Generative large language models (LLMs) offer an alternative to encoder-based clinical named entity recognition (NER), but their performance on fine-grained Japanese extraction tasks and sensitivity to generation settings remain uncertain. Methods: We compared two fine-tuned BERT-CRF baselines with nine open-weight LLMs on iCorpus, which defines 113 entity categories. The evaluation used 433 sentences from 36 test documents; 1,672 sentences were used for training. LLMs were evaluated using zero-shot prompting with and without JSON Schema constraints and three-seed QLoRA fine-tuning. Fine-tuned models were assessed under different output-token limits, including 900 and larger model-specific limits of 2,600 or 4,096 tokens. Performance was measured using sentence-level label-surface matching with relaxed and exact-surface F1. Results: The highest zero-shot relaxed F1 was 0.337, compared with 0.836-0.841 for the BERT baselines. At the larger output limits, all eight fine-tuned LLMs with at least 13B total parameters exceeded both BERT baselines (relaxed F1, 0.882-0.914; exact-surface F1, 0.840-0.880). Across three-seed means, increasing the output limit improved relaxed F1 by 0.052-0.085, alongside higher recall and fewer length-limited outputs. JSON Schema constraints changed relaxed F1 by -0.014 to +0.008 among seven models outside the two reasoning-oriented configurations, while medical-general model pairs showed no consistent advantage for medical specialization. Conclusions: On this historical Japanese case-report benchmark, task-specific fine-tuning combined with adequate generation capacity was associated with stronger LLM extraction performance. Output-token limits materially affected comparisons with BERT, whereas enforcing output structure alone did not overcome low zero-shot accuracy.

item.title: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the operator set the expected share of a clean asset's windows the running monitor escalates. A physics-policy validator checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against the decision a deterministic policy derives from the same interval. On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows the monitor cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0), escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target, while the fixed physical range it replaces leaves both attacks open. Behind a Qwen3-14B planner the composed monitors hold urgency-class injection to 0.00 and the universal sensor attack to 0.12, against 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt. An adaptive attacker defeats a Mahalanobis detector on 0.504 of windows and adversarial training on 0.485. We report an attack class the projection misses.

item.title: Multistage Contextual Optimization for Vehicle Repositioning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ride-hailing platforms reposition idle vehicles to improve spatial supply-demand balances. This problem is prediction-driven and multistage: at each stage, the platform forecasts future demand, executes current decisions, and uses the resulting state to initialize the next stage. We formulate a multistage linear program (LP) with a macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) linking accumulation to trip completion. We then develop a multistage contextual optimization approach that uses decision performance to train the prediction model. The learning problem combines multiple coupled stages, context that depends on earlier decisions, and predictions that affect the objective, the constraint matrix, and the right-hand side of the LP. We derive the exact gradient, which has three parts: parameters change forecasts and hence decisions; earlier decisions change the current decision through the inherited state; and this state also changes forecasts as context. An equivalent adjoint uses reverse vector-Jacobian products, avoiding full solution and state-parameter Jacobians. Finally, forward propagation solves many stage LPs one after another, which makes training slow. We propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of consecutive stages in parallel and repeatedly feeds each block output to the next block. We prove that the algorithm recovers the serial trajectory within a finite number of passes and that its gradient error remains bounded when it stops early. On New York City ride-hailing data, multistage contextual optimization yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error, outperforms all compared baselines from five paradigms, and even outperforms realized demand fed to the same policy. With eight workers, parallel block evaluation shortens training by a factor of 1.86 without loss of decision performance.

item.title: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.

item.title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

item.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.

item.title: PACT: Plan-Action Consistency Training by Preserving Correct Plans and Repairing Actions in GUI Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GUI agents can formulate a correct immediate plan in their reasoning yet emit an action that fails to execute it, creating an execution gap. This recurring mismatch undermines reliable task completion, as a single execution error can derail a multi-step workflow. In outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, broadcasting a negative response-level advantage across all generated tokens risks penalizing valid planning together with erroneous execution. To address this credit-assignment conflict, we introduce PACT (Plan-Action Consistency Training), a training framework that combines reference-aligned plan protection and plan-aligned action repair without altering the original scalar action reward. Using annotated reference actions to identify execution gaps, PACT protects the verified plan by masking negative policy-gradient contributions across its token span. Keeping the generated reasoning unchanged as context, it then favors the reference action over the emitted erroneous action through a preference surrogate with stop-gradient pair weights. Compared with the outcome-only baseline, PACT raises AndroidWorld task success from 60.34% to 68.97% (+8.63 pp), while improving rule-based plan-action consistency on AndroidControl High from 83.71% to 89.74% (+6.03 pp). Adapting PACT to desktop agents also improves task success from 40.92% to 44.17% (+3.25 pp) on the full 369-task OSWorld benchmark. Together, these results establish PACT as an effective credit-assignment framework for bridging execution gaps and improving task completion across mobile and desktop GUI environments.

item.title: COTTI: Contrastive Training and Time-Aware Inference for Robust Industrial Recommendation under Promotional Drift [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.22597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Promotional events shift traffic composition, purchase behavior, and the scale of conversion probabilities on different time horizons. We present \textbf{COTTI} (\textbf{CO}ntrastive \textbf{T}raining and \textbf{T}ime-aware \textbf{I}nference), an industrial recommendation framework that separates historical representation learning from event-time score adjustment. Cross-Period Contrastive Alignment (CPC) regularizes paired histories of the same user with adaptive consistency weights. Active Re-weighting (RW) controls the influence of promotional examples through historical-interest distance. Adaptive Boundary Alignment (ABA) combines stochastic prediction variability with a temporal event kernel to adjust logits while keeping predictor parameters fixed. We analyze the weighted objective and bound ABA-induced probability and ranking changes. On Fliggy data, COTTI attains an offline AUC of 0.8127, compared with 0.8101 for TEN and 0.8123 for TEN with ABA. Cross-category analysis reveals improved discrimination alongside declines in paid-item recall for novel categories. End-to-end measurements give a p99 latency of 38.9\,ms and throughput of 14,700 requests/s; enabling ABA adds 2.2\,ms to p99. A ten-day online experiment against the serving HDR model yields relative gains of 3.14\% in conversion rate and 2.68\% in revenue per mille. Together, these results characterize the trade-off between aggregate prediction, novel-category discovery, and serving cost in promotional recommendation.

item.title: Improved Convergence Rates for Stochastic Multi-Gradient Descent which Close the Gap: A Proof by AI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.18174v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For smooth nonconvex stochastic multi-objective optimization, stochastic multi-gradient descent (SMG) computes an approximate steepest common descent direction of the objectives from stochastic gradients. Under standard assumptions, this note establishes a new convergence rate for SMG in terms of the squared Pareto-stationarity (PS) measure. With a constant stepsize and linearly growing mini-batches, the expected squared empirical PS measure at the algorithm's output is $\tilde{O}(T^{-1})$ after $T$ iterations. This improves on the $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/4})$ bound obtained by Chen et al. (JMLR, 2024) for linearly growing batches, without requiring bounded gradients. Here, $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ suppresses logarithmic factors. The key to the rate improvement is to exploit the Lipschitz continuity of the PS measure, defined by the norm of the multi-gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) direction, rather than the $(1/2)$-H\"older continuity of the MGDA direction used by Chen et al. (2024). For variants of MoCo and MoCo+ with exact MGDA updates and constant batch sizes, the analysis gives expected squared empirical PS rates of $O(T^{-1/2})$ and $\tilde{O}(T^{-2/3})$, respectively. These bounds match the corresponding single-objective momentum rates up to logarithmic factors. The proof was accidentally discovered while the author was preparing homework for a graduate course: ChatGPT 5.4 Thinking Extended generated the initial proof strategy for the main SMG result in response to an author-written homework-solution prompt; the author then verified and reorganized the resulting argument. The appendices document the prompt, summarize the student submissions with LLM disclosures, and present additional proofs and results on momentum-based stochastic MGDA.

item.title: RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deployed LLMs field hundreds of millions of conversations a day and refuse a non-trivial fraction of user requests, yet the user-side cost of refusal, whether users disengage and by how much, is unmeasured on any production model: a blind spot for the consumer-facing platforms built on them. A/B-testing refusal is ethically and operationally constrained on frontier-lab products and unavailable to third-party platforms deploying these models through a fixed API. We introduce RAW, a method that uses LLM stochasticity as a natural experiment: at near-identical prompts in any existing log, the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, and that variation identifies the causal user-side effect of refusal. Applying the method to 15 deployed LLMs in LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat, with user-clustered inference, we find that for about half of the models we can measure precisely, a refusal costs 3 to 17 pp of subsequent re-engagement; the rest show no distinguishable effect, among them one deployment whose positive point estimate we trace to persistent users retrying the refused request. Our contribution is the measurement method, which runs on any deployed model from logs alone for about \$0.30 per 1,000 conversations. We release labels, moderation scores, prompt embeddings, and pipeline code.

item.title: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hoel (2021) proposed that dreams distort replayed experience so that the brain does not overfit to recent events. We test this hypothesis on an LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) that stores what it learns in a text memory and rewrites that memory each night from the day's conversation transcript. The agent goes through ten simulated days of conversation built from LongMemEval. We corrupt 5, 10, 20 or 40 percent of the transcript's turns before each nightly rewrite in one of two ways. Detail corruption changes one or two details in a turn to plausible wrong ones, or replaces the turn with one by the same speaker from an earlier day. Random-text corruption replaces half of the selected turns with a passage of Moby-Dick and inserts Moby-Dick words into the other half. A size limit on the memory, rising from 19,500 to 117,000 tokens over ten nights, set from human free-recall data, forces it to forget. We learned that corruption did not help the agent apply what it learned in earlier conversations to new tasks in any of 30 runs (ten conditions, three different conversation histories). Replacing details in 40 percent of turns lowered recall from 76 to 60 percent. Random text had no consistent effect on recall, with a paired difference of 0 $\pm$ 2 points at 40 percent, because the model recognized it as corrupted and left it out of memory. Replaced details were stored as fact even when another turn held the correct value, and the agent answered 40 percent of those questions correctly, compared with 75 percent without corruption. These results suggest that a pretrained model can separate corrupted text from real events, so a fair test needs a learner that cannot make this separation as easily, such as a model fine-tuned on the corrupted days or an agent whose days take place in an invented world.

item.title: Literary Language Mashup: Curating Fictions with Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to human evaluation of literary fictions by employing LLMs themselves as evaluators within the GrAImes framework. We apply this methodology to assess human-written and AI-generated microfictions in Spanish, to five PhD professors in literature and sixteen literary enthusiasts, and to short stories in both Spanish and English. By comparing the evaluations performed by LLMs with those of human judges, we examine the degree of alignment and divergence between both perspectives, thereby assessing the feasibility of LLMs as auxiliary literary evaluators. Our analysis focuses on the alignment of responses from LLMs with those of human evaluators, providing insights into the potential of LLMs in literary assessment. The conducted experiments reveal that while LLMs cannot be regarded as substitutes for human judges in the evaluation of literary microfictions and short stories, with a Krippendorff's alpha reliability coefficient less than 0.66, they can serve as a valuable tool that offers an initial perspective on the editorial quality of the texts in question. Overall, this study contributes to the ongoing discourse on the role of artificial intelligence in literature, underlining both its methodological constraints and its potential as a complementary resource for literary evaluation.

item.title: From Preference Data to Personalization: Tracing Sycophancy in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sycophancy in large language models is often measured as agreement with the user, yet agreement can be appropriate when the user's claim is valid, their preference is genuine, or their experience warrants acknowledgment. We study sycophancy as inappropriate agreement: validating a claim, preference, or self-assessment when the context calls for correction, qualification, or resistance. We introduce a validity-aware sycophancy grader and SycoDrift, a persona-targeted evaluation set of 3,298 validity-annotated probes with controlled annotations for user openness and stakes. We use this framework to analyze three sources of agreement pressure: human preference data, automated judge specification, and in-context personalization. First, preference for validating responses in human datasets (Chatbot Arena, HH-RLHF, Community Alignment) is weak and concentrated where agreement is often appropriate. Second, in a selected-value, single-model experiment, emphasized judge rubrics produce consistent but modest increases relative to paired suppressed rubrics, demonstrating a plausible mechanism for training-time amplification. Third, in off-policy evaluations across 14 models, inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement, with the largest effect from matched user profiles placed directly before the query.

item.title: Consistency Is Not Correction: Separating Confidence, Abstention, and Recovery in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21651v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A controller that resamples an answer, escalates to a larger model, or abstains is usually justified by a confidence signal. Three claims about such a signal do not follow from one another: it ranks answers (discrimination), it supports withholding some of them (selective prediction), and it changes an answer for the better (correction utility). We give an exact decomposition of the third into gated recoveries minus gated harms, which bounds whether a comparison can succeed before it is run: a gate that only replaces a proposal can act only where the base policy was already wrong, so the initial error count caps the discordant pairs any correct gate can produce. When that cap falls below the count a paired test needs, the experiment cannot return a positive result for a working mechanism, nor distinguish one from a gate that never fired. We measure all three targets on two model scales and find the bound binds. In a small-model suite a perturbation-agreement verifier reaches within-policy AUROC 0.990 (95% interval [0.95, 1.00]) while every episode outcome matches single-sample decoding at 4.32 times the call count. In a controlled 840-episode study no verifier replaced the proposal on any of the 60 GSM8K decisions, so that comparison tested nothing; the entire GSM8K gain across six controllers is one task, and it is the task whose identical temperature-zero repeats disagreed, making it the one answer the service does not reproduce. On the diagnostic set the gate could reach four errors while the test needed six, so even a perfect gate had no significant result available. We report two checks that would have caught this before any budget was spent, and show that tie handling in rankings, tied selection cutoffs, and unequal output limits each move a headline number in the same dataset. The binding constraint on this literature is measurement resolution, not the choice of signal.

item.title: Evaluating Semantic Insensitivity in Financial Sentiment Analysis: Implications for Sustainable Financial Decision-Making [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Financial sentiment analysis is critical for automated trading, portfolio management, and risk assessment, heavily relying on models like FinBERT. Despite high benchmark accuracy, these models remain vulnerable to subtle adversarial text modifications, threatening the integrity of algorithmic decision-making. In this paper, we propose Agent-driven Semantic Inversion (ASI), a novel adversarial attack framework targeting financial sentiment models through domain-specific semantic manipulation. Utilizing an LLM-powered multi-agent pipeline, our approach identifies eligible financial news sentences and applies targeted lexical substitutions. We empirically evaluate ASI against FinBERT, one of the most widely deployed financial sentiment models. Our results reveal a striking vulnerability: the attack successfully deceived FinBERT in 90.85% of eligible cases, with the model frequently maintaining its original sentiment prediction despite the fundamental inversion of financial performance indicators. Through qualitative analysis and token-level investigation, we demonstrate that FinBERT critically over-relies on contextual keywords and syntactic patterns rather than true logical comprehension of financial semantics. Our findings highlight the urgent need for logic-aware, robust financial NLP models to ensure the reliability of automated decision-making systems.

item.title: AdaFlowLite: Scalable and Non-blocking Inference on Asynchronous Mobile Data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rise of mobile devices equipped with numerous sensors, such as LiDAR and cameras, has driven the adoption of multi-modal deep intelligence for distributed sensing tasks, such as smart cabins and driving assistance. However, the arrival time of mobile sensory data vary due to modality size and network dynamics, which can lead to delays (if waiting for slow data) or accuracy decline (if inference proceeds without waiting). Moreover, the diversity and dynamic nature of mobile systems exacerbate this challenge. In response, we present a shift to \textit{opportunistic} inference for asynchronous distributed multi-modal data, enabling inference as soon as partial data arrives. While existing methods focus on optimizing modality consistency and complementarity, known as modal affinity, they lack a \textit{computational} approach to control this affinity in open-world mobile environments. % \sysname pioneers the formulation of structured cross-modality affinity in mobile contexts using a hierarchical analysis-based normalized matrix. This approach accommodates the diversity and dynamics of modalities, generalizing across different types and numbers of inputs. Employing an multi-modal lightweight Swin Transformer (MMLST), \sysname facilitates real-time and flexible data imputation, adapting to various modalities and downstream tasks without retraining. Experiments show that \sysname significantly reduces inference latency by up to 80.4\% and enhances accuracy by up to 62.1\%, while achieving nearly a 50\% reduction in energy consumption, outperforming status quo approaches. Also, this method can enhance LLM performance to preprocess asynchronous data.

item.title: TIBECG: Temporal Information Bottleneck for Lead-Specific Demographic Privacy in ECG Waveform Release [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transmitting an electrocardiogram (ECG) waveform can expose demographic information beyond an intended diagnostic task. We evaluate TIBECG, an architectural temporal information bottleneck, on individual leads extracted from hospital twelve-lead recordings. A 2,302,337-parameter processor varies its latent length while retaining the same nine-score consistency objective, without age or sex labels in protector fitting. Across 6,386 recordings, ten folds, 12 leads and 21 lengths, retrospective selections retained at least 95% of each lead's clean macro-F1. Their weaker age/sex interval gain exceeded the best eligible conventional transformation on all leads, by a median 22.08 percentage points. The implemented sampling-rate comparison shows that direct downsampling usually suppresses demographic inference more strongly but at a larger loss of diagnostic utility, whereas TIBECG favors utility preservation. Selection stability also varies by lead. Lower latent Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence does not reliably rank residual sex leakage at a fixed length. These findings support lead-specific evaluation of waveform processing, not validated consumer deployment or expert-readable reconstruction. When the waveform-input diagnostic classifier is hosted as part of a proprietary cloud service rather than deployed on the device, waveform transmission is required to obtain its scores.

item.title: Stop Early, Stay Simple: Evidence Acquisition for Power System Fault and Attack Diagnosis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21695v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diagnostic models for cyber-physical power systems usually inspect every telemetry source for every event, although some events are clear from one source and others need several. We ask when a learned policy for choosing that evidence is worth its added complexity. To answer this, we present ActiGrid, a benchmark framework for active evidence acquisition that pairs a classifier trained to tolerate missing modalities with a Double Deep Q-Network (DQN), which either requests another source or stops and diagnoses but never operates grid actuators. On the public TU Delft digital substation and MSU/ORNL power system attack benchmarks, we compare the DQN with fixed subsets and orders, calibrated entropy stopping, a greedy value of information rule, and tree ensembles trained per subset. The learned policy does adapt to what it observes, yet it is statistically indistinguishable from entropy stopping on TU Delft and Pareto dominated by simple controls on MSU/ORNL, while compact subset classifiers outperform it while reading fewer sources on both benchmarks. Entropy stopping run over those subset classifiers reaches the highest mean Macro-F1 on TU Delft (0.928 while reading 57% of the sources) but brings no saving over a static three source subset on MSU/ORNL, where no method exceeds 0.45 Macro-F1. Selective acquisition can pay off, but on these benchmarks it does not need a learned policy.

item.title: Watermark Evidence under Open-Weight LLM Modification: Exact Bounds for Low-Rank Output Watermarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21702v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Open-weight language models can continue generating after their released weights are modified, while a watermark verifier still scores outputs against the original base and marked models. We study how such modifications change the evidence available to an OpenStamp-style verifier. At each shared prefix, we represent the modification as a residual in the next-token logits. We derive an exact finite-vocabulary lower bound on the expected log-likelihood-ratio evidence under a residual-span constraint, along with a sharp span-only deviation bound. We also characterize the first-order evidence shift through a covariance term with an explicit second-order remainder, and determine the residual span needed to reach a target evidence level. For sequence-level detection, we derive an exact conditional exponential-moment bound and combine it with a supermartingale argument and a distribution-free order-statistic tolerance bound. This yields a high-confidence upper bound on miss probability after attack selection on calibration data and evaluation on independent certification continuations. In experiments with OpenStamp on Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, INT8 quantization and 30% pruning retain test true-positive rates of 85.6-94.8%, while 500-step LoRA fine-tuning lowers them to 28.8% and 11.6%. The covariance prediction tracks the measured mean LoRA evidence drift on both models, with no remainder-bound violations across 160,000 test prefixes. Additionally, we observe zero false positives among 500 base-model continuations per model. Through these theoretical and empirical results, the current research provides a better understanding of watermark robustness to model-editing/tuning attacks.

item.title: Margin Dynamics for Large Language Model Alignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Practitioners choose among LLM alignment methods largely by trial and error. We provide a theoretical foundation: each pairwise method defines a vector field on the probability simplex that governs how the model redistributes mass between preferred and dispreferred completions. Projecting onto a single preferred/dispreferred pair reduces this to a one-dimensional margin ODE with a closed-form solution. These solutions reveal that DPO margins grow without bound (logarithmically as $O(\log t)$ in the gradient-flow limit) while IPO margins converge to a finite $1/(2\tau)$; that label noise induces a qualitative phase transition in DPO (unbounded $\to$ bounded) but affects IPO only quantitatively; and that gradient concentration under asymmetric weighting governs trainability at scale. We confirm all three predictions across five model families spanning four benchmarks. The closed-form solutions also enable principled method design: we prove that adding any label smoothing $\varepsilon > 0$ to SimPO creates a finite margin attractor at $\Delta^* = \beta^{-1}\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)$, while $\varepsilon = 0$ (standard SimPO) has no attractor. We test this across three models (8B-9B) and confirm the prediction: the theory-derived configuration (TPO-S, $\varepsilon = 0.05$) is competitive with the strongest baselines, attaining the highest mean IFEval score among the compared methods on all three, validating that the predicted finite attractor is a usable operating point rather than proposing a new state-of-the-art loss.

item.title: SimAI: Mechanistic User Simulation through Psychological Network Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21808v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Realistic user simulation enables the study of human interactions when direct experimentation is costly or potentially harmful. However, existing simulators largely overlook the psychological mechanisms that drive user behavior. We introduce SimAI, a framework for mechanistic user simulation that models how psychological factors interact to shape user responses. To overcome the challenge of supervising open-ended behavior, we propose a graph reconstruction objective that provides graph-level rewards based on how well simulated conversations reflect the underlying psychological relationships. To support this approach, we construct PSYCHE, a dataset of 18,576 profile-network pairs derived from 516 psychotherapy cases. Automatic evaluations show that SimAI achieves greater simulation and behavioral diversity than existing patient simulators while maintaining strong profile alignment. In an interactive study with 30 mental-health professionals and trainees, SimAI receives the highest average ratings for conversational authenticity, realistic help-seeking behavior, and clinical training utility. Beyond simulation quality, SimAI enables realistic clinical training and uncovers safety failures in prolonged AI interactions with vulnerable users. Code is available at https://github.com/behavioral-data/ANGEL-UserSim.

item.title: TUSI: A Citation-Grounded Graph-Based Benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in Persian law remains challenging because benchmarks lack realism, grounding, and coverage of legal reasoning. Existing resources are either synthetically generated from statutory texts, lacking natural information needs, or derived from informal legal question--answer sources without explicit linkage to authoritative legal documents, making them unsuitable for rigorous evaluation of grounded legal reasoning. To address this gap, we introduce TUSI-Bench, a structured Persian legal benchmark designed for the evaluation of RAG-based systems. TUSI-Bench is built upon a multi-layered legal knowledge framework containing 7,261 legal articles and integrating codified statutes, legal commentaries, doctrinal writings, and Supreme Court unification rulings. We also construct a legal knowledge graph linking articles and concepts for structure-aware retrieval. Based on this foundation, TUSI-Bench provides two complementary evaluation tasks: (i) TUSI-QA, an open-ended question answering benchmark containing 1,999 questions that requires grounded responses with explicit legal citations, and (ii) TUSI-Bar, a multiple-choice benchmark containing approximately 500 four-option questions derived from Iranian Bar examination questions. Furthermore, we propose a graph-based retrieval baseline that leverages relational structure within the legal knowledge graph. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating graph-based relations improves retrieval recall by up to 8 percentage points compared to standard baselines, highlighting the importance of structured legal representations for RAG systems. The proposed benchmark provides a standardized resource for evaluating grounded legal reasoning in Persian and enables future research on structured legal intelligence.

item.title: Coordination of Heterogeneous Teams with Uncertain Task Requirements [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21828v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coordinating a team of heterogeneous agents to complete tasks with unknown requirements is a challenging multi-agent planning problem. Agents differ in their ability to discover task requirements and in their ability to engage tasks, so the planner must coordinate task discovery, execution, and staging. This paper introduces a hierarchical planner that uses a graph neural network policy to assign actions to agents, then finds a path to the action's location using a shortest-path algorithm. The central part of our approach is the CAAT graph, which is a graph representation of the planning context consisting of the agents, tasks, capabilities, and actions. We demonstrate that our learned planner can jointly coordinate a heterogeneous team to simultaneously discover task requirements and complete tasks in a shorter time compared to baselines that optimize task discovery and task engagement independently. Furthermore, we show that our policy can zero-shot plan on out-of-distribution settings by training only on an outdoor map then transferring without finetuning to an indoor map with more agents, tasks, and capabilities than seen during training.

item.title: Inventa: Decentralized Self-Improving Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can generate research ideas and improve scientific discovery through iterative experimentation. However, increasing the number of agents or iterations does not automatically translate to producing more diverse or feasible ideas. Agents may converge on similar candidates, propagate unsupported claims through shared memory components and repeatedly apply search strategies that no longer yield any improvements. We introduce Inventa, a framework for automated scientific discovery that employs autonomous research units and verified shared knowledge. Each unit creates a lineage of candidate ideas using a mutator agent. A local orchestrator agent periodically adapts the mutator's harness. When progress stalls, the orchestrator agent replaces its model or restarts the idea evolution process. Verifiers evaluate each candidate idea and record verified improvements, useful components and constraint violations in a shared knowledge, the only channel between units. We evaluate Inventa on five benchmarks spanning the research cycle, covering retrieval (ScholarCatalyst), ideation (IdeaBench), proposal writing (IdeaScientist), and scientific law discovery (EurekaBench, SciLaws-Bench). It leads all five, achieving 73.6% on EurekaBench versus 56.2% for CORAL. On IdeaBench, it discovers 26.0 novel ideas per paper, compared with 18.6 for ResearchAgent, with 82% fewer model calls.

item.title: PromptPack: Training-Free Augmentation of Diffusion Editors for Intent-Aligned Spatial and Semantic Control [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many image-editing tasks require confining changes to intended spatial regions while exactly preserving user-designated source content. Instruction-driven editing pipelines often leave such user-intent underspecified, while inpainting editors condition generation on explicitly defined edit support but not on the spatial assignment of individual edit concepts. PromptPack addresses both limitations by equipping diffusion editors with two explicit 'Edit Guides': an edit-role partition that labels each pixel as 'Keep,' 'Permit,' or 'Modify' to specify where edits may occur, and a regional-prompt assignment that maps spatial regions to text prompts to specify which concepts apply where. These guides may be manually specified or, for source-object edits, automatically derived from a text-grounded SAM 3 mask. Without retraining, PromptPack injects independently embedded regional prompts into the editor's fixed-length text sequence and uses the Edit Guides to spatially mask attention, gate flow updates, and restore protected source pixels. We integrate PromptPack into FlowEdit FLUX, FlowEdit SD3, and FLUX Kontext and demonstrate improved requested-concept placement and protected-content preservation across all three integrations on PIE-Bench++. In a pairwise user study, PromptPack achieves an 87% preference rate over FlowEdit FLUX, establishing PromptPack as a practical, training-free interface for intent-aligned diffusion editing.

item.title: Cancellation-Free Constrained SquareCB for Safe Controller Selection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21880v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study constrained contextual bandits, in which a learner chooses one of $K$ actions in each round to minimize loss while keeping the expected cost of its play below a budget. Existing reductions to online regression weight the cost by a Lagrange multiplier learned from past constraint residuals, so slack in some rounds can offset violations in others. We instead run SquareCB proposed in \citep{foster2020beyond} with a rectified weight on the cost: it is zero when the estimated cost is within the budget, and otherwise just large enough to bring it back to the budget. Under realizability and Slater's condition with margin $\delta$, the algorithm attains regret $O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)}/\delta)$ and cancellation-free violation $\sum_t(V_c^{p_t}-b)^+=O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)})$, where $\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}$ is the error of the regression oracle. The same bounds hold when the budget must be met in every context, potentially adversarially chosen contexts. In controller selection for a safe-control-gym quadrotor and a BOPTEST building, the violation is 6 to 9 times lower than that of primal-dual and virtual-queue baselines, with a lower or comparable regret.

item.title: A Temporal Algebraic Framework for Data Stream Evaluation Under Delayed Labels and Distribution Shifts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In data streams, labels often arrive late or only for some instances, class prevalence drifts, and rare classes vanish from short windows. Standard evaluation then confuses a degraded decision boundary with a change in prevalence, and is biased when labels are delayed or selected by the model. We extend an algebraic framework that obtains pooled (micro) and per-class (macro) measures from one confusion matrix to streams, weighting the counts in time by exponential fading or a sliding window; the update costs O(m^2) per step, whatever the stream length, and each pooled measure stays a weighted combination of the per-class ones. Delayed and selective feedback enter as an observation mask: until its label arrives, an instance is counted with the model's calibrated class probabilities, and the bias of this interim estimate is driven by their calibration error. Audited conventions report no value for a class without verified instances. We separate prior shift from concept drift by monitoring prior-free coordinates (recall and specificity) and attribute a change in a measure to the two sources with a first-order Jacobian decomposition. On synthetic streams and four real datasets, a detector on these coordinates with a memory per class raises no excess false alarms under label shift, unlike the Jacobian alarm and error-rate detectors. The correction for delayed labels recovers recall in some real settings and is only partial for precision, specificity and F1. Twenty-five statements are checked in Lean 4, and the code is in the aggmetrics package.

item.title: ALOHA Lightning: Learning Fast and Precise Manipulation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.21919v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Learning from human demonstrations has enabled robots to acquire a wide range of manipulation skills, but learned policies typically execute far slower than ordinary humans. This speed gap is mainly due to lack of an interface for collecting demonstration data at high speed, and the difficulty in training policies that can robustly execute high-speed motions. In this paper, we present ALOHA Lightning (Flash ALOHA), a system for learning fast and precise robotic manipulation. Our system uses kinesthetic teaching to intuitively collect near-human-speed demonstrations on a backdrivable bimanual platform, yielding natural and fast trajectories. We also present a learning pipeline that enables smooth high-speed execution through test-time action smoothing and aligns the visual data distribution between data collection and deployment with masking.
